{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=automated+falsification+self+reflection+agent+axioms&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.20944/preprints202607.1126.v1\", \"title\": [\"Automated Scientific Discovery via Causal Falsification and Formal Multi-Agent Verification\"], \"abstract\": \"Scientific AI systems can generate hypotheses and explanations, but many opti-mize plausibility more than refutability. This paper presents a falsification-drivenmulti-agent framework in which specialized agents propose hypotheses, build causalmodels, design adversarial tests, and verify formal claims. The architecture com-bines hypothesis generation, causal reasoning, falsification, formal verification, andpersistent orchestration through a shared memory state that records assumptions,counterexamples, interventions, and proof obligations. By treating failed predictionsand invalid proof attempts as useful learning signals, the framework shifts discoveryfrom fluent claim production toward disciplined claim survival. On simulated dis-covery tasks, the full system improves verified discovery rate from 0.42 to 0.76 andreduces false-positive hypothesis retention from 0.31 to 0.08. Scaling experimentsshow a peak discovery quality factor of 0.83 with eight agents, supporting the prin-ciple that scientific AI should prioritize systematic refutation, causal identifiability,and machine-checkable proof.\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.1126.v1\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 7, 15]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7143760\", \"title\": [\"FalsiCite: Adaptive Falsification Agent for Traceable Miscitation Detection in Multimodal Scientific Literature\"], \"abstract\": \"The rapid expansion of scientific publication has made citation verification at scale a critical but infeasible-to-manually-perform task. Existing large language model (LLM) based citation detectors suffer from two failure modes: hallucinated references, in which models confidently cite papers that do not exist or do not say what is claimed, and confirmation-cascade bias, in which an LLM judge tends to agree with its own prior verdicts even when those verdicts are wrong. Worse, real scientific claims are rarely supported by text alone; they draw on tables, figures, and equations scattered across the full paper, and naive modality fusion underperforms when modalities contribute unequally. We propose FalsiCite, an LLM-driven agent for traceable miscitation detection in multimodal scientific literature that unifies three innovations. First, an adaptive falsification verifier generates adversarial probes to actively disconfirm citation-claim alignments and updates a calibrated Bayesian posterior, explicitly countering confirmation-cascade bias. Second, a contribution-aware dynamic modality balance module estimates per-claim, per-modality contribution weights and reweights text, table, and figure features before fusion, mitigating modality laziness. Third, a weak-to-strong verification distillation scheme leverages visual in-context learning to scale verification capability from a small fine-tuned teacher to a large frontier student verifier without additional human labels. On the CiteME benchmark, FalsiCite achieves 74.6 percent accuracy and a 3.1 percent hallucination rate, outperforming the strongest prior agent (BibAgent, 72.4 percent) while producing a fully auditable reasoning trace. On the SciVer multimodal benchmark, FalsiCite attains 73.8 percent average accuracy, closing 21.5 percent of the gap between the strongest prior vision-language model and human experts. Human evaluation confirms that 91.7 percent of FalsiCite traces are fully grounded in retrievable evidence, compared to 76.4 percent for BibAgent and 51.2 percent for an LLM-as-a-Judge baseline. Ablations show that adaptive falsification reduces the confirmation-cascade failure rate from 19.7 percent to 5.4 percent, that modality balancing adds 4.6 accuracy points on multimodal claims, and that weak-to-strong distillation reduces annotation cost by an order of magnitude while preserving verifier quality.\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7143760\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7338838\", \"title\": [\"Generative-Agent Modeling of Protest Mobilization and Preference Falsification with Large Language Models\"], \"abstract\": \"This paper presents a generative-agent architecture for agent-based modeling (ABM) of protest mobilization and preference falsification under authoritarian repression, motivated by recent social-media-mediated uprisings in South and Southeast Asia. Unlike classical threshold and spatial models, each of 1,000 agents interprets its situation through a large language model (LLM) utilizing memories of past events, and produces a natural-language justification for whether to mobilize. Preference falsification is formalized as a deterministic coefficient ω gating the divergence between internal grievance and expressed stance, and the adversarial state is a network-altering algorithm performing eigenvector-centrality-based suspension and an edge-removal shutdown (not triggered at these parameters). The identical architecture is run across three backbones: GPT-4.1-mini, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and Llama-4-Maverick-over three seeds each. The central observation is that the emergent LLM-driven layer diverges sharply despite fixed imposed dynamics: peak mobilization ranges from 23.3% (GPT-4.1-mini) to 14.8% (DeepSeek-V4-Flash) to 3.2% (Llama-4-Maverick). This ordering inverts the hidden-transcript gap, which is largest for Llama-4-Maverick (0.268). Logged justifications from high-grievance inactive agents confirm the mechanism is analogous to preference falsification: agents reach maximal internal grievance while declining public action on grounds of personal and familial risk. A control probe rules out simple incapacity, and no meaningful content-refusal effect appears in any backbone. The contribution is an architecture and observations, not a validated model of real dissent, distinguishing emergent from imposed results.\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7338838\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.3366/edinburgh/9781474422857.003.0010\", \"title\": [\"Being and Appearing: Self-falsification, Exchange and Freedom in Rousseau and Adam Smith\"], \"abstract\": \"

We are familiar with the charge that commercial society reduces exchange (social and economic) to a sort of play-acting characterized by bad faith, false consciousness, and estrangement. Rousseau famously insists that the phenomenon of not appearing as who or what one really is, of living “outside” as opposed to “within” oneself, constitutes a pervasive defect of modern society especially. Remarkably, Smith’s review of the Second Discourse included translations of relevant passages. This chapter explores what Rousseau means by I will call “self-falsification.” Passages from Smith are deployed as a way of fleshing out both the strongest version of Rousseau’s claims and the tenability of Smith’s response. The debate turns in part on how one understands freedom or agency and their connection to spectatorship, role-playing, and delusion. With the help of work by Langton and others, I reflect on Smith’s notion of agential freedom in view of Rousseau’s claims.
